clinicalPearls: The second most common form of CMT overall, caused by mutations in GJB1, which encodes the gap-junction protein connexin 32.
Inheritance is X-linked: hemizygous males are affected relatively uniformly and more severely, while heterozygous females are milder and more variable, and male-to-male transmission does not occur.
Nerve conduction shows an intermediate, often asymmetric pattern that lies between the demyelinating and axonal ranges, a useful diagnostic clue.
Distinctive transient central nervous system episodes occur: reversible white-matter dysfunction with ataxia, dysarthria or weakness, sometimes provoked by fever, exertion or high altitude.
Connexin 32 forms reflexive gap junctions in Schwann cells at the paranodes and Schmidt-Lanterman incisures, providing a radial pathway across the myelin sheath.
Onset in affected males is usually in childhood or adolescence, with distal wasting, pes cavus, foot drop and areflexia.
Diagnosis is by GJB1 sequencing; the combination of an intermediate conduction pattern and absent male-to-male transmission should prompt testing.
reference.pathophysiology: X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMTX1) is caused by mutations in GJB1, which encodes connexin 32, a gap-junction protein expressed by Schwann cells where it assembles reflexive channels that form a short radial diffusion pathway across the layers of the myelin sheath, connecting the perinuclear and periaxonal cytoplasm. Loss of these channels impairs Schwann cell-to-axon communication and myelin homeostasis, producing a neuropathy with both demyelinating and axonal features and characteristically intermediate, often asymmetric, conduction slowing. Because the gene lies on the X chromosome, hemizygous males are affected relatively uniformly and more severely, whereas heterozygous females show milder and more variable involvement reflecting random X-inactivation, and there is no male-to-male transmission. Connexin 32 is also expressed by central oligodendrocytes, which underlies the episodic, reversible central white-matter dysfunction sometimes provoked by fever, exertion or high altitude.
additionalDifferentials: CMT1A and CMT1B (autosomal dominant demyelinating neuropathies)
Acute encephalopathy or stroke, for the transient central episodes
Multiple sclerosis or acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, for the reversible white-matter lesions
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies showing intermediate, asymmetric slowing that differs between affected males and carrier females
MRI brain during or after a transient central episode (reversible white-matter change)
Detailed pedigree analysis confirming an X-linked pattern without male-to-male transmission
Assessment of potentially symptomatic female carriers
redFlags: Acute encephalopathy, ataxia or dysarthria with white-matter change, sometimes following altitude exposure, fever or exertion
Rapid asymmetric decline suggesting an alternative or superimposed pathology
Marked disability in a female, prompting reconsideration or a search for skewed X-inactivation
reference.prognosis: Affected males progress slowly to moderate disability by mid-adulthood, whereas females are often only mildly affected; the transient central nervous system episodes typically resolve fully.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting transient central white-matter episodes as stroke, multiple sclerosis or acute disseminated encephalomyelitis.
Excluding the diagnosis because a female relative is only mildly affected.
Expecting a uniform demyelinating pattern, when the conduction abnormality is intermediate and asymmetric.
Overlooking the X-linked inheritance pattern when taking and documenting the family history.
management: No disease-specific pharmacotherapy; supportive and rehabilitative care through a neuromuscular multidisciplinary team
Physiotherapy, stretching and ankle-foot orthoses for distal weakness, pes cavus and foot drop
Recognition and reassurance regarding the transient reversible central episodes, which resolve spontaneously and need only supportive care
Advice to avoid precipitants of central episodes such as high altitude, febrile illness and extreme exertion
Neuropathic pain management with gabapentinoids or tricyclic agents
Avoidance of neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine
X-linked genetic counselling including assessment of potentially symptomatic female carriers, noting the absence of male-to-male transmission
